lessons.title: Types of Hospitality & Catering Provision
lessons.description: Commercial and non-commercial providers, food service styles, and star ratings explained.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Hospitality & Catering?

The hospitality and catering industry is one of the largest sectors in the UK economy, employing around 2.9 million people and generating £130 billion in economic activity. It is the third-largest private sector employer — bigger than automotive, pharmaceuticals, and aerospace combined. To revise this topic effectively, you need to understand the difference between commercial and non-commercial provision, and the difference between residential and non-residential services.

Key Fact

Hospitality and catering provision is split into four categories: commercial residential, commercial non-residential, non-commercial residential, and non-commercial non-residential. Commercial means the business aims to make a profit. Non-commercial means the service is provided without a profit motive.

Commercial Residential Provision

Residential provision means overnight accommodation is included. Commercial residential providers aim to make a profit from guests who stay overnight. Examples include:

  • Hotels, motels and hostels — ranging from budget chains like Travelodge to luxury five-star hotels.
  • B&Bs, guest houses and Airbnb — smaller-scale accommodation, often family-run or privately owned.
  • Holiday parks, lodges, pods and cabins — self-catering or serviced accommodation in leisure settings.
  • Campsites and caravan parks — outdoor accommodation with catering facilities on site.
  • Cruise ships — floating hotels with restaurants, bars, and entertainment.

The range of commercial residential providers is broad. At one end, budget hotels like Travelodge and Premier Inn offer standardised rooms at low prices, relying on high occupancy to generate profit. At the other end, luxury boutique hotels and five-star resorts offer personalised service, fine dining, and exclusive facilities — charging significantly more per night but serving fewer guests. Airbnb has disrupted the traditional market by allowing private homeowners to rent out spare rooms or entire properties, creating competition for established hotels and B&Bs.

Commercial Non-Residential Provision

Commercial non-residential providers sell food, drink, or entertainment without offering overnight stays. Their main goal is still profit. Examples include:

  • Restaurants and bistros, cafés, tea rooms and coffee shops
  • Fast food outlets and takeaways
  • Public houses and bars
  • Pop-up restaurants and mobile food vans / street food trucks
  • Airlines and long-distance trains (in-flight or on-board catering)
  • Stadia, concert halls and tourist attractions (food concessions)
  • Vending machines

Non-Commercial Residential Provision

Non-commercial residential providers offer accommodation and meals, but making a profit is not the primary aim. The food and shelter are provided as part of a broader service. Examples include:

  • Hospitals, hospices and care homes — patients and residents need meals as part of their care.
  • Boarding schools, colleges and university residences — students live on site and are provided meals.
  • Prisons — inmates receive meals as part of their custodial care.
  • Armed forces — service personnel are housed and fed during training and deployment.

In all non-commercial residential settings, the quality of catering matters significantly even though profit is not the goal. Hospitals must provide nutritious meals that support patient recovery, and they must cater for a wide range of dietary requirements including allergies, religious preferences, and medical conditions such as diabetes. Boarding schools must provide balanced meals for growing adolescents, often serving hundreds of students three times a day. The cost of this catering is covered by the institution’s overall budget, government funding, or fees charged for the wider service.

Non-Commercial Non-Residential Provision

These providers offer food without overnight accommodation and without aiming to make a profit. The food is subsidised or provided free of charge. Examples include:

  • School, college and university canteens
  • Canteens in workplaces (subsidised by the employer)
  • Meals on wheels (delivered to people in their homes)
  • Charity-run food providers (e.g. food banks, soup kitchens)

Commercial providers charge customers for their services and aim to make a profit. They include hotels, restaurants, and takeaways. Non-commercial providers do not aim to make a profit. Their food or accommodation is part of a wider service — for example, a hospital feeds patients to support their recovery, not to earn money. Non-commercial catering is often subsidised by the government, a charity, or an employer.

Standards and Ratings

Hotels and guest houses are rated using star ratings from 1 to 5 stars. A one-star hotel offers basic accommodation, while a five-star hotel provides luxury facilities and exceptional service. These ratings help customers choose where to stay and set expectations for quality.

Key Fact

Restaurants can be rated by the AA Rosette Award (1–5 rosettes for food quality), the Michelin Star system (1–3 stars for exceptional dining), and the Good Food Guide. These ratings influence customer choice and can significantly boost a restaurant’s reputation and revenue.

Ratings give customers confidence in the quality of service they will receive. A higher rating often means a business can charge higher prices, attracting wealthier clientele. For the business, achieving a Michelin star or AA rosettes brings prestige, media attention, and increased bookings. However, maintaining high standards is expensive — staff must be highly trained, ingredients must be top quality, and facilities must be immaculate. Losing a star can damage a restaurant’s reputation significantly.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the Unit 1 exam, you will often be given a stimulus scenario describing a specific hospitality business. Read it carefully and identify whether the business is commercial or non-commercial, and residential or non-residential, before answering. For “State” questions worth 1 mark, keep your answer brief — just name the type or give one example. For “Describe” questions worth 2 marks, give a point and then develop it with a specific detail or example from the stimulus.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hospitality and catering provision is divided into four categories based on whether it is commercial or non-commercial, and residential or non-residential.
  • Commercial providers aim to make a profit (hotels, restaurants, takeaways); non-commercial providers supply food or accommodation as part of another service (hospitals, schools, armed forces).
  • Star ratings (hotels), AA Rosettes, Michelin Stars, and the Good Food Guide help customers judge quality and influence business success.

• A higher star rating allows the hotel to charge premium prices, increasing revenue and profit margins.
• Ratings bring media attention and prestige, which can attract more bookings and wealthier clientele.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the growth of non-residential commercial provision such as street food trucks and pop-up restaurants compared to traditional restaurants.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7•8 marks) Thorough evaluation with balanced analysis, developed reasoning, and a supported judgement.
Upper-mid band (5•6 marks) Good evaluation with some balance and reasoning.
Lower-mid band (3•4 marks) Some evaluation with limited development.
Lower band (1•2 marks) Basic points with little evaluation.

Indicative content:
Advantages of street food / pop-ups:
• Lower start-up costs • no long-term lease or expensive premises
• Flexibility to move to different locations and events where demand is high
• Can test new food concepts with lower financial risk
• Appeals to younger consumers who value novelty and social media appeal

Advantages of traditional restaurants:
• Established customer base and brand loyalty
• Can offer a wider menu and more formal dining experience
• Eligible for ratings (Michelin, AA Rosettes) which can boost reputation
• Permanent location builds community presence

Judgement should consider the target market, location, and business goals.

practice_questions.text: A new hotel chain is planning to open in a seaside town. Assess whether the hotel should aim for a 3-star or 5-star rating. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (9•10 marks) Comprehensive analysis of both options with a well-justified conclusion supported by evidence and reasoning.
Upper-mid band (6•8 marks) Good analysis with a clear judgement and some justification.
Lower-mid band (3•5 marks) Some analysis with partial reasoning.
Lower band (1•2 marks) Basic points with limited reasoning.

Indicative content:
3-star rating:
• Lower operating costs • less need for luxury furnishings, highly specialised staff, and premium amenities
• Broader customer base • affordable for families, couples, and budget travellers
• Seaside towns attract a wide range of visitors, many looking for affordable stays
• Easier to fill rooms during off-peak seasons due to lower prices

5-star rating:
• Can charge significantly higher room rates, increasing revenue per guest
• Attracts wealthier clientele who may spend more on dining, spa, and leisure
• Premium reputation differentiates from budget competitors
• However, much higher set-up and running costs
• Demand may be limited in a seaside town compared to a major city

Justification should weigh the target market for a seaside location, competition, seasonal demand fluctuations, and the cost implications of each rating level.

lessons.title: Food Service Styles & Residential Services
lessons.description: Table service, counter service, personal service, room types, and conference facilities.
lessons.content_html:
Types of Food Service

Hospitality and catering providers use different styles of food service depending on their type of establishment, target customers, and price point. The WJEC specification requires you to know three main categories of food service: table service, counter service, and personal service.

Key Fact

The three main categories of food service are table service (food brought to seated customers), counter service (customers collect food from a serving area), and personal service (food delivered directly to an individual, e.g. room service or home delivery).

Table Service

Table service is the most formal category. Customers sit at a table and waiting staff bring food to them. There are five types of table service you need to know:

  • Plate service — the most common type. Food is plated in the kitchen and carried to the table by waiting staff. Used in most restaurants.
  • Family-style service — dishes are placed in the centre of the table and diners help themselves. Common in informal restaurants and family gatherings.
  • Silver service — food is presented on silver platters and served to each guest by waiting staff using a spoon and fork. A highly skilled and formal method.
  • Guéridon service — food is prepared, carved, or flambéed at the table from a trolley. It creates a theatrical dining experience. Often seen in high-end restaurants.
  • Banquet service — a pre-set menu served to a large number of guests at a formal event, such as a wedding or awards ceremony. All courses are timed carefully.

Plate service requires less skill from waiting staff and is cost-effective, making it the most widely used. Silver service and Guéridon service require highly trained staff and are expensive to run, but they create an exclusive dining experience that justifies premium prices. Family-style is informal and suits casual dining, while banquet service is efficient for large events because the same meal is served to everyone at the same time.

Counter Service

Counter service means customers collect their food from a serving point rather than being served at a table. It is faster and requires fewer staff than table service. The three types are:

  • Cafeteria service — customers move along a counter selecting food items from a display. Common in workplace canteens and schools.
  • Buffet service — food is laid out on tables or counters, and customers serve themselves. Used at events, hotels, and all-you-can-eat restaurants.
  • Fast food service — customers order at a counter (or drive-through) and food is prepared and served quickly. Examples include McDonald’s and KFC.

Counter service is popular because it reduces labour costs — fewer waiting staff are needed since customers serve themselves or collect their food. It also increases speed of service, which suits busy environments like school lunch halls and motorway service stations. However, the dining experience is less personal, and customers may feel rushed. Buffet service in particular carries food safety risks because food is left out for extended periods, so temperature controls and hygiene procedures are critical.

Personal Service

Personal service delivers food directly to an individual, wherever they are. The four types are:

  • Tray or trolley service — food is delivered on a tray or trolley, typically in hospitals, care homes, or on aircraft.
  • Vending — automated machines dispense food and drinks. Found in offices, hospitals, and transport hubs.
  • Home delivery — food is prepared at a restaurant or kitchen and delivered to the customer’s home. Services like Deliveroo and Just Eat have made this increasingly popular.
  • Takeaway — customers order food and collect it themselves to eat elsewhere.

Residential Services

Residential hospitality providers offer accommodation alongside their catering. The WJEC spec requires you to understand the different room types and additional services that en-suite residential providers offer.

Key Fact

Room types include single, double, king, family, and suite. Rooms may have en-suite bath or shower facilities (private bathroom in the room) or shared facilities (bathroom shared with other guests).

Refreshments & Additional Facilities

Residential providers typically offer a range of refreshment options:

  • Breakfast — included in many hotels and B&Bs (continental or full cooked).
  • Lunch and evening meals — available in the hotel restaurant.
  • 24-hour room service — food delivered to the guest’s room at any time, often at premium prices.

Many residential providers also offer conference and function facilities for business meetings, weddings, and events. These can be a significant source of revenue. Leisure facilities such as spas, gyms, and swimming pools attract guests and can justify higher room rates.

Additional facilities such as conference rooms, spas, and restaurants generate extra revenue beyond room bookings. A hotel with a spa can attract guests who might otherwise stay at a competitor. Conference facilities bring business customers who often book midweek when leisure demand is lower, improving occupancy rates throughout the year. Leisure facilities also support higher star ratings, which in turn allow the hotel to charge higher prices.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The exam often uses a scenario about a specific hospitality business and asks you to recommend a suitable food service style. Make sure you can match each service type to the right context — for example, silver service suits a formal hotel dining room, while cafeteria service suits a busy school canteen. Always justify your choice by explaining why it is appropriate for that particular business.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Food service falls into three categories: table service (plate, family-style, silver, Guéridon, banquet), counter service (cafeteria, buffet, fast food), and personal service (tray/trolley, vending, home delivery, takeaway).
  • Residential services include room types (single through to suite), refreshment options (breakfast to 24-hour room service), and additional facilities like conferences and leisure.
  • The choice of food service style depends on the type of establishment, target customer, and price point.

• Reduces the need for trained waiting staff
• However, harder to control portions (guests may take too much)
• May not suit guests who expect a more formal dining experience

Justification should consider the B&B•s size, number of guests, the owner•s staffing resources, the type of clientele (families vs business travellers), and cost implications.

lessons.title: Job Roles & the Kitchen Brigade
lessons.description: Front of house roles, housekeeping, the kitchen brigade hierarchy, and personal attributes.
lessons.content_html:
Working in Hospitality & Catering

The hospitality and catering industry offers a huge variety of job roles, from front of house positions that interact directly with customers to behind-the-scenes kitchen and housekeeping roles. The WJEC specification groups these into four areas: front of house, housekeeping, the kitchen brigade, and management. You also need to know the personal attributes, qualifications, and experience employers look for.

Front of House Roles

Front of house refers to the parts of a hospitality business where staff interact directly with customers. Key front of house roles include:

  • Front of house manager — oversees the entire front of house operation, ensures high standards of service, and handles customer complaints.
  • Head waiter — supervises waiting staff, coordinates table service, and ensures the dining room runs smoothly.
  • Waiting staff — take orders, serve food and drinks, and clear tables.
  • Maître d’hôtel — the chief host in a formal dining room, responsible for greeting guests and managing reservations.
  • Concierge — assists hotel guests with bookings, recommendations, and special requests.
  • Receptionist — handles check-in and check-out, takes bookings, and provides information to guests.
  • Valets — provide personal service to guests, such as parking cars or handling luggage.

Housekeeping Roles

Housekeeping staff ensure the accommodation and public areas of a hospitality establishment are clean, safe, and well maintained. Key roles include:

  • Chambermaid — cleans and prepares guest rooms, changes bedding, and restocks supplies.
  • Cleaner — maintains cleanliness in public areas, corridors, and facilities.
  • Maintenance staff — repairs and maintains the building, fixtures, and equipment.
  • Caretaker — oversees the general upkeep of the premises.

The Kitchen Brigade

The kitchen brigade is a structured hierarchy of chefs and kitchen workers. Each person has a specific role, ensuring the kitchen runs efficiently. From the most senior to the most junior, the roles are:

Key Fact

The kitchen brigade hierarchy (top to bottom): Executive Chef → Sous Chef → Chef de Partie → Commis Chef → Pastry Chef → Kitchen Assistant → Apprentice → Kitchen Porter / Plongeur.

  • Executive Chef — the most senior chef, responsible for the entire kitchen operation, menu planning, budgets, and staff management.
  • Sous Chef — the second-in-command, deputises for the executive chef and supervises daily cooking.
  • Chef de Partie — a section chef responsible for a particular area of the kitchen (e.g. sauces, fish, meat).
  • Commis Chef — a junior chef who works under a chef de partie, learning the skills of a specific section.
  • Pastry Chef — specialises in desserts, breads, and pastries.
  • Kitchen Assistant — assists with food preparation tasks such as peeling, chopping, and weighing ingredients.
  • Apprentice — a trainee learning kitchen skills while working towards a qualification.
  • Kitchen Porter / Plongeur — responsible for washing up, keeping the kitchen clean, and general cleaning tasks.

Management roles coordinate different departments within a hospitality business. Food and beverage manager — oversees the restaurant, bar, and room service operations. Housekeeping manager — manages the cleaning and maintenance team. Marketing manager — promotes the business through advertising, social media, and partnerships to attract customers.

Understanding the kitchen brigade is important because it shows how a professional kitchen is organised for maximum efficiency. Each role has a clear set of responsibilities, and every member of the team knows who they report to. In a busy restaurant serving hundreds of covers per evening, this structure prevents confusion and ensures dishes are prepared consistently to the same standard. Without the brigade system, communication would break down, orders would be missed, and food quality would suffer. Even smaller kitchens use a simplified version of this hierarchy, with the head chef taking on multiple senior roles.

Personal Attributes Employers Look For

The hospitality industry requires staff to have specific personal qualities. Employers look for people who are:

  • Organised and punctual — shifts must start on time, and tasks must be completed efficiently.
  • Hardworking and flexible — the industry involves long hours, weekend work, and adapting to busy periods.
  • Hygienic — food safety and cleanliness are essential, especially in kitchen and housekeeping roles.
  • Friendly, pleasant, and calm — staff must remain professional even when dealing with difficult customers.
  • Good communicator and team player — hospitality relies on teamwork and clear communication between departments.
  • Good people skills and a willingness to learn and develop — customer-facing roles require empathy and a desire to improve.
Key Fact

The WJEC spec lists 12 personal attributes: organised, hardworking, punctual, hygienic, pleasant, calm, friendly, good communicator, team player, good people skills, willingness to learn, and flexible.

Employers also look for relevant qualifications and experience. Apprenticeships allow people to train on the job while earning a wage and gaining a qualification. Experience in the sector — such as a part-time job or summer employment — shows an employer that the candidate understands the industry. School, college, or university qualifications relevant to hospitality and catering (including this WJEC course) demonstrate knowledge and commitment.

  • The kitchen brigade is a hierarchy with specific responsibilities at each level, from menu planning (executive chef) to washing up (kitchen porter / plongeur).

lessons.title: Working Conditions & Employment
lessons.description: Contract types, wages vs salaries, benefits, seasonal work, and supply and demand.
lessons.content_html:
Types of Employment Contracts

The hospitality and catering industry uses a range of employment contracts to match the varied and often unpredictable demands of the sector. The WJEC specification requires you to understand five types of contract and their implications for both employers and employees.

Key Fact

The five types of employment contract in the hospitality industry are: casual, full-time permanent (or temporary), part-time (or temporary), seasonal, and zero-hours.

  • Full-time permanent — the employee works a set number of hours each week (usually 35–40 hours) with an ongoing contract. This provides job security and stable income. Temporary full-time contracts cover a fixed period, such as maternity cover.
  • Part-time — the employee works fewer hours than full-time, often on set days. This suits people with other commitments, such as students or parents. Temporary part-time contracts cover short-term needs.
  • Casual — the employee has no guaranteed hours and works when needed. Common for event catering or busy weekends.
  • Seasonal — employment for a specific time of year when demand is high, such as summer in a seaside hotel or Christmas in a restaurant.
  • Zero-hours contract — the employer offers work when available, but there is no guarantee of hours. The employee can accept or decline. This gives employers flexibility but provides little job security for the worker.

Remuneration & Benefits

Remuneration means the total payment and benefits an employee receives for their work. In hospitality and catering, remuneration can take several forms:

  • A salary — a fixed annual amount paid monthly, regardless of exact hours worked. More common for management roles.
  • A wage (hourly) — payment based on the number of hours worked. The most common form for waiting staff, kitchen assistants, and housekeeping.
  • Tips, bonuses, and rewards — additional payments from customers (tips) or the employer (bonuses for good performance). Tips can form a significant part of income for waiting staff.

Employees in the industry may also receive benefits such as:

  • Holiday entitlement — paid time off (full-time workers are entitled to a minimum of 28 days including bank holidays).
  • Pension — contributions towards the employee’s retirement savings. All employers must offer a workplace pension scheme.
  • Sickness pay — payment when the employee is too ill to work. Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) is the legal minimum.
  • Rates of pay — the hospitality industry must comply with the National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage set by the government.

A salary is a fixed annual amount divided into equal monthly payments. It provides financial stability because the employee knows exactly how much they will earn each month. A wage is calculated by multiplying the number of hours worked by the hourly rate. Wage earners benefit when they work overtime (extra hours at a higher rate), but their income varies if hours fluctuate. In hospitality, senior managers and executive chefs tend to receive salaries, while waiting staff, kitchen assistants, and housekeeping are typically paid hourly wages.

Supply & Demand in the Industry

The hospitality and catering industry normally provides more part-time positions than full-time ones. Demand for staff fluctuates significantly depending on several factors:

Key Fact

Supply and demand for staff is affected by four main factors: peak times (busy evenings, weekends), large events (weddings, festivals, conferences), seasonal times (summer holidays, Christmas), and the location of the provision (tourist areas need more staff in high season).

During peak times, such as Friday and Saturday evenings, restaurants need more waiting staff, chefs, and bar staff. During quiet midweek periods, fewer staff are needed. Large events like weddings, conferences, and music festivals create a sudden spike in demand for temporary workers.

Seasonal work is especially common in tourist areas. A seaside hotel may employ double the staff in July and August compared to January. Ski resorts, Christmas markets, and summer festivals all create seasonal employment. Workers may move between different seasonal jobs throughout the year.

The location of a business also affects staffing. A restaurant in central London faces intense competition for workers and may need to offer higher wages to attract staff. A rural pub may struggle to find employees because fewer people live nearby.

For employers: Flexible contracts (casual, zero-hours, seasonal) allow them to match staffing levels to demand, reducing labour costs during quiet periods. However, high staff turnover can increase recruitment and training costs, and a lack of committed staff may reduce service quality.

For employees: Flexible work can suit students or people with other commitments. Tips and overtime can boost income during busy periods. However, unpredictable hours make it difficult to plan finances, and zero-hours workers may not receive the same benefits as permanent staff. Job insecurity can cause stress and reduce motivation.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When the exam gives you a scenario about a hospitality business struggling with staffing, think about supply and demand. Is it a seasonal issue? A location issue? Consider recommending a specific contract type and explain why it suits the situation. For “Evaluate” questions, always weigh up both sides — for example, zero-hours contracts give employers flexibility but can lead to poor staff retention.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The hospitality industry uses five main contract types: casual, full-time permanent/temporary, part-time/temporary, seasonal, and zero-hours.
  • Remuneration includes salaries, hourly wages, tips, bonuses, holiday entitlement, pensions, and sickness pay.
  • Demand for staff fluctuates based on peak times, large events, seasonal patterns, and business location — this is why the industry relies heavily on part-time and flexible workers.

Negative impacts:

Judgement should consider whether the hotel could diversify to attract off-season guests (conferences, special events) to provide more stable employment.

practice_questions.text: A hotel manager is reviewing the pay and benefits package for staff. Assess whether offering higher wages or better benefits (such as longer holidays and a pension) would be more effective at attracting and retaining staff. Justify your answer.

• However, significantly increases labour costs, which are already one of the biggest expenses in hospitality
Better benefits:
• Longer holidays improve work-life balance, reducing burnout in a demanding industry
• Pensions provide long-term financial security, showing the employer values staff
• Benefits build loyalty and reduce turnover, saving recruitment costs
• However, benefits are less immediately noticeable than a pay rise — younger workers may prioritise wages over pensions
Judgement should consider the type of staff (junior vs senior), the local job market, competitor offerings, and the hotel’s budget. A combination of competitive wages and meaningful benefits is likely the most effective approach.

lessons.title: Business Success Factors
lessons.description: Costs, profit calculations, the economy, technology, environmental impact, and media influence.
lessons.content_html:
Costs in Hospitality & Catering

Running a hospitality or catering business involves three main types of cost. Understanding these is essential because controlling costs directly affects whether the business makes a profit or a loss.

Key Fact

The three main costs in hospitality and catering are: labour costs (wages, salaries, training, National Insurance), material costs (food ingredients, drinks, cleaning products), and overheads (rent, utilities, insurance, equipment, marketing).

  • Labour costs — the cost of employing staff, including wages, salaries, training, and employer National Insurance contributions. Labour is typically the largest cost in hospitality, often accounting for 25–35% of revenue.
  • Material costs — the cost of raw materials such as food ingredients, beverages, and cleaning supplies. For a restaurant, food costs are usually 28–35% of the selling price.
  • Overheads — all other costs of running the business, including rent, utility bills (gas, electricity, water), insurance, equipment maintenance, and marketing.

Calculating Profit

The WJEC specification requires you to understand two types of profit calculation:

Gross profit is calculated by subtracting material costs (cost of ingredients/goods) from revenue (total sales). It shows how much money is left after paying for the raw materials used to make the products sold.

$$\text{Gross Profit} = \text{Revenue} - \text{Material Costs}$$

Net profit is calculated by subtracting all costs (materials, labour, and overheads) from revenue. It shows the actual profit the business keeps after every expense has been paid.

$$\text{Net Profit} = \text{Revenue} - \text{Total Costs (Materials + Labour + Overheads)}$$

A restaurant has total revenue of £500,000 per year. Its material costs are £150,000, labour costs are £175,000, and overheads are £100,000.

Gross profit = £500,000 − £150,000 = £350,000

Net profit = £500,000 − (£150,000 + £175,000 + £100,000) = £500,000 − £425,000 = £75,000

This means the restaurant keeps £75,000 after all expenses. The gross profit of £350,000 looks large, but once labour and overheads are deducted, the actual profit is much smaller — showing why cost control is vital.

The Economy & Its Impact

The strength of the economy has a direct impact on hospitality businesses. When the economy is strong and people have more disposable income, they spend more on eating out, holidays, and leisure. When the economy weakens (during a recession), customers cut back on non-essential spending, and hospitality businesses suffer.

Two specific economic factors you need to know are:

  • Value Added Tax (VAT) — a government tax added to the price of goods and services. If VAT increases, prices rise for customers, which may reduce demand. If the government lowers VAT for hospitality (as it did temporarily during the COVID-19 pandemic), businesses can lower prices or increase profit margins.
  • Value of the pound and exchange rates — if the pound is strong, foreign holidays become cheaper for UK tourists, meaning fewer people holiday in the UK (bad for UK hotels). A weak pound makes the UK cheaper for foreign visitors, boosting tourism. However, a weak pound also makes imported ingredients more expensive, increasing material costs for caterers.

Environmental Impact

Hospitality and catering businesses have a responsibility to minimise their environmental impact. The WJEC spec identifies two key areas:

Key Fact

Seasonality means using ingredients that are in season locally, reducing the need for importing food from abroad (which increases carbon emissions from transport). Sustainability involves the three Rs: reduce (minimise waste and energy use), reuse (repurpose materials where possible), and recycle (separate waste for recycling).

Technology in Hospitality

New technology is transforming how hospitality businesses operate. The spec identifies several positive impacts:

  • Cashless systems — contactless card and mobile payments speed up transactions, reduce queues, and improve security by handling less cash.
  • Innovative digital technology — apps for ordering and booking, web-based reservation systems, key card access for hotel rooms, and digital menus (QR code menus became widespread during the pandemic).
  • Software — stock management, payroll, rota planning, and accounting software streamline operations and reduce human error.

Online booking systems allow customers to reserve tables or rooms 24/7, even outside business hours. This increases bookings and reduces the need for reception staff to handle phone calls. Stock management software tracks ingredient usage in real time, helping chefs order the right amounts and reduce food waste. Payroll software automates wage calculations, ensuring staff are paid correctly and on time. However, technology requires investment and staff training, and system failures can disrupt the entire operation.

Media & Its Impact

Media can have both positive and negative impacts on hospitality and catering businesses. The four types of media you need to know are:

  • Printed media (newspapers, magazines) — a positive review in a food magazine can boost bookings; a negative review can drive customers away.
  • Broadcast media (television, radio) — TV shows like MasterChef inspire people to eat out and try new restaurants. A restaurant featured positively on TV may see a surge in demand.
  • Internet and social media (websites, Instagram, TripAdvisor) — positive online reviews attract customers, but a viral negative review can cause serious damage. Social media is fast, free to use, and reaches millions of people.
  • Competition from other establishments — businesses must be aware of what competitors are doing. If a rival opens nearby or runs a promotion, the business may need to respond with its own marketing or improvements.

Social media is both an opportunity and a threat for hospitality businesses. On the positive side, platforms like Instagram allow restaurants to showcase their food with visually appealing photos, reaching potential customers for free. Positive TripAdvisor reviews build trust and encourage new visitors. Many businesses now use social media advertising targeted at specific demographics and locations. However, one negative review or complaint can go viral, damaging the business’s reputation far more quickly than a newspaper review ever could. Businesses must actively manage their online presence, responding promptly to complaints and encouraging satisfied customers to leave reviews.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For profit calculation questions, always show your working — even if you get the final answer wrong, you can still pick up method marks. For “Evaluate” and “Extended Response” questions on success factors, structure your answer around multiple factors (costs, economy, technology, media, environment) and explain how they connect. A strong conclusion that weighs up which factor matters most will push your answer into the top mark band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The three main costs are labour, materials, and overheads. Gross profit = revenue minus material costs; net profit = revenue minus all costs.
  • The economy (strength, VAT, exchange rates), environmental sustainability (seasonality, reduce/reuse/recycle), and technology (cashless systems, apps, software) all affect business success.
  • Media (print, broadcast, internet, competition) can have powerful positive or negative effects — social media is both an opportunity and a threat.

lessons.title: Front & Back of House Operations
lessons.description: Front of house and kitchen workflows, equipment, documentation, and dress codes.
lessons.content_html:
Front of House & Back of House

Every hospitality and catering establishment is divided into two main areas: front of house and back of house. Front of house covers everything the customer experiences directly — reception desks, dining rooms, counter service areas, and bars. Back of house is where the food is prepared, stored, and managed behind the scenes. Both areas must work together smoothly to deliver a positive customer experience.

Key Fact

Front of house includes reception, seating areas, counter service, and the bar. Back of house includes the kitchen, storage, wash areas, and staff changing rooms.

Workflow of the Front of House

The front of house workflow ensures customers are greeted, seated, served, and billed efficiently. In a restaurant, this typically follows a clear sequence: the customer arrives at reception, is shown to their table, receives menus, places an order, is served food and drinks, and finally pays the bill. Each stage must run smoothly to avoid delays and complaints.

Different front of house areas serve different purposes. The reception is the first point of contact — it sets the tone for the whole visit. The seating area is where customers eat, and it must be clean, well-laid, and comfortable. Counter service areas are used in cafeterias and fast food outlets where customers collect food themselves. The bar serves drinks and may also be a waiting area before meals.

Workflow of the Catering Kitchen

The kitchen workflow follows a logical sequence designed to maintain food safety and efficiency. The WJEC specification identifies seven key areas within a catering kitchen:

1. Delivery area — where raw ingredients and supplies arrive. Deliveries are checked against order forms for quality and quantity. 2. Staffing area — where staff change into uniforms and store personal belongings. 3. Wash area — for washing hands and sanitising before entering the kitchen. 4. Storage area — dry stores, fridges, and freezers, each kept at correct temperatures. 5. Preparation and cooking area — where food is prepared and cooked, the largest and busiest part of the kitchen. 6. Serving area (the pass) — where finished dishes are checked and handed to waiting staff. 7. Washing/cleaning area — where used equipment and crockery are cleaned and sanitised.

Equipment and Materials

A professional catering kitchen uses a wide range of equipment. The specification divides this into three categories:

Large equipment includes conventional ovens, glass chillers, floor-standing food mixers, deep fat fryers, hot water urns, walk-in fridge-freezers, standing bain marie units, steamers, pass-through dishwashers, glass washers, and hot plates. These are expensive to buy and maintain, so they must be used correctly and kept in good working order.

Small equipment covers utensils such as knives, chopping boards (colour-coded for food safety), pans, whisks, thermometers, and measuring jugs. Materials for cleaning include sanitisers, cloths, mops, and anti-bacterial sprays. A first aid kit and safety materials (fire blankets, fire extinguishers) must also be available at all times.

Key Fact

Kitchen equipment falls into three groups: large equipment (ovens, fryers, walk-in fridges), small equipment (utensils, thermometers), and cleaning/safety materials (sanitisers, first aid kit, fire blankets).

Documentation and Administration

Running a catering kitchen requires careful paperwork. The specification identifies several key documents:

Stock controlling systems track what ingredients are in storage and when they need reordering. Ordering documents are sent to suppliers to request new stock. Delivery notes arrive with each delivery and are checked against the order to confirm the correct items and quantities have been received. Invoices are bills from suppliers that must be checked and paid. Food safety documentation includes temperature logs, cleaning schedules, and allergen records. Health and safety documentation covers risk assessments, accident forms, and COSHH records.

Accurate documentation protects the business in several ways. If a customer becomes ill, food safety records can show that correct procedures were followed. Stock control prevents waste and reduces costs. Delivery notes and invoices ensure the business only pays for what it actually received. During an Environmental Health Officer inspection, well-kept records demonstrate legal compliance and can help avoid prosecution or closure.

Dress Code

Dress codes differ between front and back of house. Front of house staff typically wear smart, clean uniforms that reflect the establishment’s brand — this might be a shirt and tie in a fine-dining restaurant or a branded polo shirt in a casual café. Hair should be neat and jewellery minimal. The aim is to look professional and create a positive first impression.

Back of house staff wear protective clothing for hygiene and safety. This includes chef’s whites (jacket, trousers, and apron), a chef’s hat or hairnet to prevent hair falling into food, non-slip safety shoes, and blue plasters if they have cuts (blue so they are visible if they fall into food). Jewellery and nail varnish are not allowed in the kitchen because they could contaminate food.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about front and back of house, always link your points to either customer experience (front) or food safety and efficiency (back). For “Describe” questions worth 2 marks, give a clear statement plus a developed point. For longer “Explain” questions, use a chain of reasoning: state the point, explain why it matters, then link it to the impact on the business or customer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Front of house (reception, dining, counter, bar) is what the customer sees; back of house (kitchen, storage, wash areas) is where food is prepared and managed behind the scenes.
  • The kitchen workflow follows a logical sequence from delivery through to the washing/cleaning area, and equipment is grouped into large, small, and cleaning/safety categories.
  • Accurate documentation (stock control, delivery notes, invoices, food safety and health & safety records) is essential for efficiency, legal compliance, and customer safety.

lessons.title: Customer Requirements & Meeting Specific Needs
lessons.description: How hospitality venues meet customer needs, rights, dietary requirements, and changing expectations.
lessons.content_html:
Understanding Customer Requirements

Hospitality and catering businesses exist to serve customers. To succeed, they must understand what their customers need and adapt their provision accordingly. The WJEC specification identifies several categories of customer requirement: customer needs, customer rights and inclusion, lifestyle and dietary needs, customer expectations, and customer demographics.

Customer Needs

At the most basic level, customers need three things from hospitality and catering provision: catering (food and drink of an appropriate quality), equipment (cutlery, crockery, seating, and facilities), and accommodation (a clean, comfortable room if staying overnight). A customer visiting a restaurant expects clean cutlery, a comfortable chair, and well-prepared food. A hotel guest expects a clean room with fresh bedding, functioning heating, and access to meals.

Key Fact

The three basic customer needs in hospitality and catering are: catering (food and drink), equipment (cutlery, furniture, facilities), and accommodation (rooms in residential establishments).

Customer Rights and Inclusion

Every customer has the right to be treated fairly regardless of their background. Hospitality businesses must meet the requirements of equality legislation, ensuring no one is discriminated against. This includes making reasonable adjustments for customers with disabilities — for example, providing wheelchair ramps, accessible toilets, menus in Braille or large print, and hearing loops at reception desks.

Inclusion means ensuring all customers can access and enjoy the services offered. A restaurant that only has stairs to its entrance excludes wheelchair users. A hotel that offers no allergen information on its menu puts allergic customers at risk. Businesses that fail to be inclusive not only break the law but also lose potential customers and damage their reputation.

Lifestyle and Dietary Needs

Modern customers have a wide range of lifestyle and dietary needs that hospitality providers must cater for. Lifestyle choices include vegetarianism, veganism, and religious dietary requirements (such as halal or kosher food). Nutritional needs vary depending on age, health conditions, and activity levels — a child needs different portion sizes and nutrients compared to an elderly adult.

Dietary needs include medical conditions that restrict what a person can eat. Customers with coeliac disease need gluten-free options. Those with lactose intolerance cannot have dairy products. Some customers are diabetic and need meals with controlled sugar content. Hospitality businesses must be prepared to adapt their menus and communicate clearly about what each dish contains.

Restaurants now commonly label dishes with allergen symbols (such as “GF” for gluten-free or “V” for vegan). Many offer separate allergen menus on request. Hotels provide breakfast buffets with clearly labelled options including dairy-free milk, gluten-free bread, and fresh fruit. Airlines offer special meals (halal, kosher, vegetarian, vegan) that must be pre-ordered. School canteens display nutritional information and allergen charts. Failure to meet dietary needs can lead to serious illness — or even death in the case of severe allergies.

Time available is another factor. A customer on a lunch break may only have 30 minutes, so they need quick service. A couple celebrating an anniversary may want a leisurely three-course meal. Businesses must offer options that suit different time constraints — from grab-and-go sandwiches to full tasting menus.

Customer Expectations

Customer expectations go beyond basic needs. The specification identifies several factors that shape what customers expect:

Service — customers expect polite, efficient, and knowledgeable staff. A fine-dining restaurant is expected to have more formal, attentive service than a fast food outlet. Value for money — customers judge whether the price they pay matches the quality they receive. A budget hotel is not expected to have a spa, but it is expected to be clean. Trends — customer tastes change over time; plant-based menus, street food concepts, and sustainability are all current trends that businesses must respond to.

Key Fact

Customer expectations are shaped by: service quality, value for money, current trends, awareness of competition, media influence, environmental concerns, and seasonality.

Competition from other providers keeps standards high — if one restaurant offers free Wi-Fi and another does not, customers may choose the one that does. Media influence plays a huge role: a positive review on TripAdvisor or a feature on a TV food programme can boost bookings, while a negative social media post can cause lasting damage. Environmental concerns mean customers increasingly expect businesses to reduce food waste, use sustainable packaging, and source ingredients locally. Seasonality affects both what customers want (hot food in winter, salads in summer) and how busy venues are (coastal hotels peak in summer).

Customer Demographics

Demographics are the characteristics of a customer group. The specification identifies four key demographic factors:

Age — a children’s menu with smaller portions and simpler flavours differs from an adult tasting menu. Elderly customers may need softer food or larger print on menus. Location — a business in a tourist area will attract different customers to one in a residential suburb. Accessibility — some customers need step-free access, hearing loops, or menus in alternative formats. Money available — a customer with a limited budget will choose differently from one with a large disposable income. Businesses must understand their target demographic to offer appropriate provision.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In scenario-based questions, identify the specific customer described (their age, dietary needs, budget, time constraints) and explain how the business should adapt its provision to meet those needs. The best answers link each adaptation to a clear benefit for the customer and the business. For “Explain” questions worth 4 or 6 marks, develop your points with “because” and “therefore” connectives.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Customers have basic needs (catering, equipment, accommodation) plus rights to equality and inclusion that businesses must legally uphold.
  • Lifestyle and dietary needs (vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, halal, kosher) require businesses to adapt their menus and communicate allergen information clearly.
  • Customer expectations are shaped by service quality, value for money, trends, competition, media, environmental concerns, and seasonality — and demographics (age, location, accessibility, budget) determine who the customers are.

lessons.title: Health & Safety Legislation
lessons.description: Health and safety laws, risk assessments, and HACCP principles for the workplace.
lessons.content_html:
Why Health & Safety Matters

The hospitality and catering industry involves sharp knives, hot ovens, heavy equipment, and hazardous cleaning chemicals. Without proper health and safety measures, employees and customers are at serious risk of injury or illness. UK law places responsibilities on both employers and employees to maintain a safe working environment. The WJEC specification requires you to know five key pieces of legislation, understand risk levels, and be able to apply HACCP principles.

The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

This is the main piece of health and safety legislation in the UK. It places a duty of care on employers to provide a safe working environment, safe equipment, adequate training, and protective clothing. Employees must follow safety procedures, use equipment correctly, report hazards, and not put themselves or others at risk. The Act applies to every workplace, including kitchens, restaurants, and hotels.

Key Fact

The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 is the overarching law. Employers must provide safe premises, equipment, and training. Employees must follow procedures, use equipment properly, and report hazards.

COSHH — Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002

COSHH requires employers to assess and control the risks from hazardous substances in the workplace. In hospitality, this covers cleaning chemicals (oven cleaners, bleach, sanitisers), gases, dust, and biological agents such as bacteria. Employers must identify which hazardous substances are used, assess the risks, provide protective equipment (gloves, goggles), train staff in safe handling, store chemicals correctly (locked cupboards, away from food), and keep records.

Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992

These regulations cover the lifting, carrying, pushing, and pulling of heavy objects. In a kitchen, staff regularly move heavy boxes of supplies, large pans of hot liquid, and catering-sized equipment. The regulations require employers to avoid hazardous manual handling where possible, assess the risk of any handling that cannot be avoided, and reduce the risk of injury by providing trolleys, training in correct lifting technique, and ensuring loads are not too heavy for one person.

PPER — Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 1992

PPER requires employers to provide suitable personal protective equipment free of charge where risks cannot be controlled by other means. In hospitality and catering, this includes oven gloves for handling hot trays, safety goggles when using cleaning chemicals, non-slip shoes to prevent slips on wet kitchen floors, and cut-resistant gloves when using mandolins or meat slicers. Employees must use the PPE provided and report any damage.

RIDDOR — Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013

RIDDOR requires employers to report certain serious workplace incidents to the Health and Safety Executive (HSE). Reportable incidents include deaths, major injuries (broken bones, amputations, burns requiring hospital treatment), injuries that prevent an employee from working for more than seven consecutive days, work-related diseases, and dangerous occurrences (near misses that could have caused serious harm). Reports must be made without delay, and records kept for at least three years.

The specification requires you to understand how risks are classified. Low risk — unlikely to cause harm, or harm would be minor (e.g. a paper cut from a menu). Medium risk — could cause moderate harm and is reasonably likely (e.g. a slip on a wet floor causing bruising). High risk — likely to cause serious injury or death (e.g. a deep fat fryer fire or a severe allergic reaction). Risk assessments consider who might be harmed (employers, employees, suppliers, customers) and what level of risk they face. The higher the risk, the more control measures are needed.

Documentation: Accident Forms and Risk Assessments

Employers must keep two key types of health and safety documentation. Accident forms record what happened, who was injured, when and where it occurred, and what action was taken. They create a legal record and help identify patterns (e.g. repeated burns from the same oven). Risk assessments identify hazards, assess who might be harmed and how seriously, and set out the control measures in place to reduce the risk. Risk assessments must be reviewed regularly and updated when circumstances change.

Key Fact

Employers are responsible for the health and safety training of all staff. This includes induction training for new staff, ongoing refresher training, and specific training on hazards relevant to each role.

HACCP — Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points

HACCP is a systematic approach to food safety. It requires businesses to identify every stage of food production where something could go wrong (a critical control point), and put measures in place to ensure risks are removed or reduced to safe levels. For example, a critical control point might be checking the temperature of delivered meat — if it arrives above 8°C, it must be rejected.

The WJEC specification requires you to be able to: 1. Identify critical control points and ensure risks are removed or reduced to safe levels. 2. Decide what actions to take if something goes wrong (corrective actions — e.g. reject a delivery, re-cook food to the correct temperature). 3. Complete a HACCP document that records the hazard, the critical control point, the control measure, and the corrective action. 4. Complete records to show that procedures are working (e.g. temperature logs checked daily, cleaning schedules signed off). HACCP is a legal requirement for all food businesses in the UK.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For legislation questions, always state the full name and year of the Act or regulation. A common mistake is writing “the COSHH law” instead of “Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002.” For HACCP questions, use specific examples — describe a real critical control point (e.g. checking delivery temperatures) rather than writing vaguely about “checking food.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Five key pieces of legislation protect workers and customers: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974, COSHH 2002, Manual Handling 1992, PPER 1992, and RIDDOR 2013.
  • Risk assessments classify hazards as low, medium, or high risk, and must be completed and reviewed regularly. Accident forms create a legal record of incidents.
  • HACCP is a systematic food safety approach that requires businesses to identify critical control points, set control measures, define corrective actions, and keep records.

lessons.title: Food Safety: Bacteria, Allergens & Intolerances
lessons.description: Food poisoning bacteria, the 14 allergens, food intolerances, and labelling laws.
lessons.content_html:
Causes of Food-Related Ill Health

Food can make people ill in four main ways: through bacteria (food poisoning), allergies (immune system reactions to specific foods), intolerances (difficulty digesting certain substances), and chemicals (contamination from cleaning products or pesticides). This lesson focuses on the specific bacteria, allergens, and intolerances named in the WJEC specification, plus the food labelling laws that help protect consumers.

Food Poisoning Bacteria

The specification requires you to know seven specific bacteria that cause food poisoning. Each bacterium is found in different foods and conditions:

Bacillus cereus — commonly found in rice, pasta, and starchy foods. It produces toxins when cooked food is left at room temperature too long. Reheating does not destroy the toxin. Campylobacter — the most common cause of food poisoning in the UK. Found in raw or undercooked poultry, unpasteurised milk, and untreated water. Clostridium perfringens — found in soil and the intestines of animals. Grows in large batches of food (stews, gravies) that are cooked slowly and not cooled quickly enough. E. coli (Escherichia coli) — found in raw or undercooked beef, unpasteurised milk, and contaminated water. Can cause very serious illness, especially in young children and the elderly.

Listeria — found in soft cheeses, pâté, and pre-packaged salads. Unusual because it can grow at refrigerator temperatures. Particularly dangerous for pregnant women, as it can cause miscarriage. Salmonella — found in raw poultry, eggs, and dairy products. Destroyed by thorough cooking but can survive in undercooked food. Staphylococcus aureus — carried on human skin, especially in the nose and throat. Transferred to food through poor hand hygiene, sneezing, or touching food with infected cuts. The toxin it produces is heat-resistant, so reheating does not make the food safe.

Key Fact

The seven food poisoning bacteria are: bacillus cereus (rice/pasta), campylobacter (poultry), clostridium perfringens (stews/gravies), E. coli (raw beef), listeria (soft cheese/pâté), salmonella (poultry/eggs), and staphylococcus aureus (transferred from human skin).

The 14 Allergens

A food allergy is an immune system reaction to a specific food protein. Reactions can range from mild (rash, itching) to life-threatening (anaphylaxis). UK food law requires all food businesses to declare the presence of 14 specific allergens in their products:

The 14 allergens are: cereals containing gluten (wheat, rye, barley, oats), crustaceans (prawns, crab, lobster), eggs, fish, peanuts, soybeans (soya), milk (dairy), nuts (almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, cashews, pecans, Brazil nuts, pistachios, macadamia nuts), celery, mustard, sesame seeds, sulphur dioxide and sulphites (above 10mg/kg), lupin, and molluscs (mussels, oysters, squid, snails).

Key Fact

There are 14 allergens that must be declared by law. They include cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, peanuts, soybeans, milk, nuts, celery, mustard, sesame seeds, sulphur dioxide/sulphites, lupin, and molluscs.

Food Intolerances

A food intolerance is different from an allergy. It does not involve the immune system and is not life-threatening, but it can cause significant discomfort. The specification identifies four key intolerances:

Gluten intolerance (coeliac disease) — the body cannot digest gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. It damages the lining of the small intestine, causing bloating, diarrhoea, and poor nutrient absorption. Lactose intolerance — the body lacks the enzyme needed to digest lactose (the sugar in milk). Symptoms include bloating, stomach cramps, and diarrhoea after consuming dairy products. Aspartame sensitivity — aspartame is an artificial sweetener found in diet drinks and sugar-free products. Some people experience headaches, dizziness, or digestive problems after consuming it. MSG (monosodium glutamate) sensitivity — MSG is a flavour enhancer used in many processed foods and Chinese cooking. Some people report headaches, sweating, and chest tightness after consuming it.

An allergy involves the immune system and can be life-threatening (anaphylaxis). Even a tiny amount of the allergen can trigger a reaction. An intolerance does not involve the immune system and is not life-threatening, but causes uncomfortable symptoms like bloating, stomach pain, and diarrhoea. People with intolerances can often tolerate small amounts of the food without a serious reaction. Both require hospitality businesses to provide clear information about ingredients.

Food Labelling Laws

UK food labelling laws require all pre-packaged food to clearly list ingredients, highlight the 14 allergens (usually in bold or a different colour), display a use-by or best-before date, and include nutritional information. Since October 2021, Natasha’s Law (named after Natasha Ednan-Laperouse, who died from an allergic reaction to a Pret A Manger baguette) requires food prepared and packed on the same premises where it is sold (such as sandwiches made in-store) to carry a full ingredients list with allergens emphasised. Restaurants and takeaways must also be able to provide allergen information when asked, either on the menu or through trained staff.

The specification also requires you to be aware of food safety legislation and food hygiene more broadly. Food safety legislation sets the legal framework that all food businesses must follow — covering everything from how food is stored and prepared to how staff handle ingredients. Good food hygiene means following practices that prevent contamination: washing hands before and after handling food, keeping raw and cooked food separate, cleaning surfaces regularly, and ensuring food is cooked to the correct temperature. Together, labelling laws, food safety legislation, and hygiene practices form a chain of protection that keeps customers safe from food-related ill health.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to identify food poisoning bacteria, always match the bacterium to its food source — for example, “campylobacter, commonly found in raw or undercooked poultry.” For allergen questions, remember the number 14 and group them logically (grains, seafood, dairy, nuts, others). The difference between allergy and intolerance is a common exam question — always mention that allergies involve the immune system and can cause anaphylaxis, while intolerances do not.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Seven named bacteria cause food poisoning: bacillus cereus, campylobacter, clostridium perfringens, E. coli, listeria, salmonella, and staphylococcus aureus — each linked to specific foods.
  • There are 14 allergens that must be declared by law, and four named food intolerances (gluten, lactose, aspartame, MSG). Allergies involve the immune system and can be fatal; intolerances cause discomfort but are not life-threatening.
  • Food labelling laws (including Natasha’s Law) require clear allergen information on all food products, whether pre-packaged or prepared on-site.

Limitations:
• Labels rely on consumers reading them — some people may not check.
• ‘May contain’ warnings are voluntary and used inconsistently, causing confusion.
• Restaurants only need to provide allergen information when asked, which relies on the customer knowing to ask.
• Small businesses may lack training to implement labelling correctly.
Judgement: Food labelling laws have significantly improved consumer safety, particularly since Natasha’s Law. However, they are only effective if businesses comply and consumers engage with the information provided.

lessons.title: Symptoms, Prevention & the Environmental Health Officer
lessons.description: Visible and non-visible symptoms of food illness, prevention methods, and the role of the EHO.
lessons.content_html:
Symptoms of Food-Induced Ill Health

When a person eats contaminated food or food they are allergic or intolerant to, they develop symptoms. The WJEC specification divides these into visible symptoms (those you can see) and non-visible symptoms (those the person feels internally but others cannot observe). Being able to recognise these symptoms is important for hospitality staff, as it helps them respond quickly and appropriately.

Visible Symptoms

Visible symptoms are those that can be observed by others. The specification lists the following:

Anaphylactic shock — a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction causing swelling of the throat and tongue, difficulty breathing, and a rapid drop in blood pressure. Requires immediate treatment with an adrenaline auto-injector and emergency medical care. Bloating — the stomach appears swollen and distended. Breathing difficulties — wheezing, shortness of breath, or gasping, often associated with allergic reactions. Chills — shivering and feeling cold, often accompanying a fever caused by bacterial infection.

Diarrhoea — frequent, loose, or watery stools, a very common symptom of food poisoning. Facial swelling — swelling around the eyes, lips, or face, typically an allergic reaction. Pale or sweating skin — the person looks pale, clammy, or sweaty. Rash — red, raised, or itchy patches on the skin. Vomiting — the body’s way of expelling contaminated food. Weight loss — longer-term symptom associated with ongoing conditions like coeliac disease or persistent food intolerance.

Key Fact

Visible symptoms include: anaphylactic shock, bloating, breathing difficulties, chills, diarrhoea, facial swelling, pale or sweating skin, rash, vomiting, and weight loss.

Non-Visible Symptoms

Non-visible symptoms are felt by the person but cannot be seen by others. The specification lists: constipation, feeling sick (nausea), painful joints, stomach-ache, weakness, and wind/flatulence. These symptoms are just as important as visible ones — a customer who feels nauseous or has severe stomach cramps is suffering, even though their symptoms are not immediately obvious to staff.

Preventative Control Measures

Prevention is far better than cure. The specification identifies three key control measures that hospitality businesses must follow to prevent food-induced ill health:

1. Preventing Cross Contamination

Cross contamination is the transfer of harmful bacteria or allergens from one food to another. It is one of the most common causes of food poisoning in catering. There are three types: direct (raw meat dripping onto cooked food in a fridge), indirect (using the same chopping board for raw chicken and salad without washing it), and hand-to-food (touching raw meat then handling bread without washing hands).

Prevention measures include: using colour-coded chopping boards (red for raw meat, blue for fish, green for salad, yellow for cooked meat, white for dairy, brown for vegetables), storing raw meat on the lowest shelf of the fridge (below cooked and ready-to-eat food), washing hands thoroughly between handling different foods, using separate utensils for raw and cooked food, and cleaning and sanitising work surfaces between tasks.

Red — raw meat. Blue — raw fish. Green — salad and fruit. Yellow — cooked meat. White — dairy and bakery products. Brown — vegetables. Using the correct colour-coded board for each food type prevents bacteria from raw foods being transferred to ready-to-eat foods. This is a simple but highly effective food safety measure used in professional kitchens.

2. Correct Temperature Control

Bacteria multiply rapidly in the danger zone between 5°C and 63°C. Temperature control is critical at every stage of the food chain:

Delivery — chilled food should arrive below 8°C and frozen food below −18°C. Reject any delivery outside these temperatures. Storage — fridges should be set between 0°C and 5°C, freezers at −18°C or below. Preparation — food should be kept out of the fridge for the minimum time possible during preparation. Cooking — food must reach a core temperature of at least 75°C to kill harmful bacteria. Service — hot food must be kept above 63°C. If food drops below this, it should be reheated to 75°C or discarded.

Key Fact

Key temperatures: Fridge 0–5°C | Freezer −18°C | Danger zone 5–63°C | Core cooking temperature at least 75°C. Bacteria multiply most rapidly in the danger zone.

3. Preventing Physical Contamination

Physical contamination occurs when a foreign object gets into food. Examples include hair, plasters (which is why blue plasters are used — they are easier to spot), pieces of packaging, glass, metal fragments from worn equipment, jewellery, and pests (insects, rodent droppings). Prevention measures include wearing hairnets, removing jewellery, maintaining equipment in good condition, keeping the kitchen clean and pest-free, and inspecting ingredients on delivery.

The Environmental Health Officer (EHO)

The Environmental Health Officer (EHO) is a local authority official who ensures food businesses comply with food safety and environmental health legislation. The WJEC specification lists seven key EHO responsibilities:

1. Inspecting businesses for food safety standards — checking hygiene, storage, equipment, and documentation. 2. Collecting evidence including food samples for testing, photographs, and conducting interviews with staff. 3. Following up outbreaks of food poisoning — investigating the source and taking action to prevent further cases. 4. Enforcing environmental health laws and following up complaints from the public. 5. Giving evidence in prosecutions when businesses have broken the law. 6. Maintaining evidence — keeping accurate, detailed records for potential court proceedings. 7. Submitting reports to the local authority on their findings and any enforcement action taken.

After an inspection, the EHO awards a food hygiene rating from 0 (urgent improvement necessary) to 5 (very good). This rating must be displayed at the premises and is published online so customers can check it before visiting. A low rating can seriously damage a business’s reputation and customer numbers.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on symptoms, state whether each symptom is visible or non-visible — this shows the examiner you understand the classification. For temperature questions, always include specific numbers (5°C, 63°C, 75°C, −18°C) rather than vague answers like “the right temperature.” When discussing the EHO, list specific responsibilities rather than just saying “they check food safety.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Visible symptoms (vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, anaphylaxis) can be observed; non-visible symptoms (nausea, stomach-ache, weakness, flatulence) are felt by the person but hidden from others.
  • The three preventative control measures are: preventing cross contamination (colour-coded boards, separate storage), correct temperature control (danger zone 5–63°C, core cooking 75°C), and preventing physical contamination (hairnets, blue plasters, pest control).
  • The EHO inspects businesses, collects evidence, investigates outbreaks, enforces laws, gives court evidence, maintains records, and submits reports — awarding food hygiene ratings from 0 to 5.

practice_questions.text: Describe one way a catering kitchen can prevent cross contamination.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for identifying + 1 mark for development:
• Use colour-coded chopping boards (1) — different colours for different food types (e.g. red for raw meat, green for salad) to prevent bacteria transferring between foods (1).
• Store raw meat on the lowest shelf of the fridge (1) — this prevents raw meat juices dripping onto cooked or ready-to-eat food stored below (1).
• Accept other valid prevention methods with development.

practice_questions.text: Explain why temperature control is important at every stage of the food chain, from delivery to service.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a developed explanation:
• Bacteria multiply rapidly in the danger zone between 5°C and 63°C (1). At delivery, chilled food must arrive below 8°C or it should be rejected (1). During storage, fridges must be between 0°C and 5°C to keep food below the danger zone (1). Food must be cooked to a core temperature of at least 75°C to kill harmful bacteria, and served hot above 63°C (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the Environmental Health Officer (EHO) in maintaining food safety standards.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough explanation covering multiple EHO responsibilities with clear reasoning.
Mid band (3-4): Sound explanation of at least two responsibilities.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification with limited development.
Indicative content:
• The EHO inspects food businesses for hygiene, storage, equipment, and documentation standards.
• They collect evidence (food samples, photographs, interviews) during inspections.
• They investigate outbreaks of food poisoning to identify the source and prevent further cases.
• They enforce environmental health laws and can prosecute businesses that break the law.
• They award food hygiene ratings (0–5) that are displayed publicly, influencing customer choice.
• Their role protects the public by ensuring food businesses maintain safe standards.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of colour-coded chopping boards in preventing food poisoning in a busy catering kitchen.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Thorough analysis and evaluation with a supported judgement.
Mid band (4-6): Sound analysis with some evaluation.
Lower band (1-3): Basic points with limited development.
Indicative content:
Effective:
• Colour-coded boards provide a simple, visual system that is easy for all staff to follow, even in a busy kitchen.
• They prevent indirect cross contamination by ensuring raw meat bacteria do not transfer to ready-to-eat foods.
• The system is widely recognised and standardised across the industry.
• Relatively low cost to implement.
Limitations:
• Only effective if staff are trained and consistently use the correct board — human error can undermine the system.
• Boards must be cleaned and sanitised properly between uses, or bacteria can still spread.
• Colour-coded boards alone are not sufficient — they must be combined with hand washing, separate utensils, and correct storage.
• Damaged or worn boards must be replaced regularly as scratches harbour bacteria.
Judgement: Colour-coded boards are a highly effective and cost-efficient measure, but they are only one part of a wider food safety system. Their effectiveness depends on staff training, compliance, and being used alongside other control measures.

practice_questions.text: A restaurant has received a food hygiene rating of 1 (major improvement necessary) from the EHO. Discuss what the restaurant should do to improve its rating.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (8-10): Comprehensive discussion covering multiple food safety improvements with developed reasoning.
Mid band (4-7): Good discussion of several improvements.
Lower band (1-3): Basic identification of improvements.
Indicative content:
• Review and improve temperature control — check fridges are 0–5°C, freezers at −18°C, and implement regular temperature logging.
• Address cross contamination risks — implement/enforce colour-coded chopping board system, separate raw and cooked food storage.
• Improve cleaning schedules and ensure all surfaces are sanitised between tasks.
• Review HACCP documentation — ensure all critical control points are identified with corrective actions recorded.
• Retrain all staff on food safety, hand hygiene, and allergen awareness.
• Complete risk assessments and update health and safety documentation.
• Ensure COSHH compliance — chemicals stored correctly, away from food.
• Address any physical contamination risks — hairnets, blue plasters, pest control.
• Request a re-inspection from the EHO once improvements have been made.
• Use the EHO’s report to prioritise the most critical issues first.
